title: Comparing Quantum Circuit Born Machines and Restricted Boltzmann Machines for Generative Modelling of Financial Data
abstract_summary: This preprint investigates and compares quantum and classical generative models for synthetic data generation on a real-world financial dataset of correlated currency pairs. The authors train quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) — using the Sinkhorn divergence and other methods — on simulators and Rigetti quantum hardware, finding that simulated QCBMs match or outperform RBMs as model scale and precision increase, and that higher entanglement in trained QCBM circuits correlates with observed advantages. They also report partial training of a 28-qubit QCBM on Rigetti hardware and discuss implications and future directions.
methodology_description: The paper compares a quantum circuit Born machine (QCBM) against a classical restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) for generative modelling of FX financial data. They convert FX spot prices (daily log-returns) into binary vectors by discretizing each currency pair to j bits of precision, producing datasets for i currency pairs (nv = i * j visible bits). For fairness they fix the total number of trainable parameters in both models: the QCBM is implemented as a hardware-efficient ansatz with layers of single-qubit Ry rotations and native CZ entangling gates matching Rigetti Aspen topologies, and the RBM is constrained by fixing its pairwise weights randomly and training only local bias terms so the number of trainable parameters matches the QCBM. The primary training objective for the QCBM is the Sinkhorn divergence (regularized optimal transport) between model and data distributions, with analytic gradients obtained via the parameter-shift rule; optimization is performed with Adam (also vanilla gradient descent tested). The RBM is trained by maximizing data log-likelihood with gradients computed from model expectations, using QxSQA (a GPGPU-accelerated PIMC simulated quantum annealer) for sampling Boltzmann-like distributions during training. Additional/alternative training objectives and methods explored include Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), adversarial (discriminator-based) training (random-forest discriminator with 1000 estimators from scikit-learn used as benchmark and for adversarial loop) and a gradient-free genetic algorithm for small instances. Evaluation uses a random-forest discriminator error (higher error == better generator), Sinkhorn divergence, QQ-plots of marginals and analysis of Meyer–Wallach entangling capability of trained QCBM circuits. Experiments are run both in classical simulation and on Rigetti QPUs (various Aspen sublattices, up to a 28-qubit instance), with multiple independent runs (e.g. 5 repeats) to compute means and standard deviations.

Sinkhorn divergence (regularized optimal transport) as cost
experimental_setup: Simulations and hardware experiments. Dataset: FX spot prices (daily log-returns) for 4 currency pairs from 1999-2019 (5070 samples), discretized to j bits per currency pair (2..16 bits used), forming binary vectors of length nv = i * j for i=2,3,4 pairs; subsets of pairs used to form problem instances. QCBM: hardware-efficient ansatz of L layers, each layer = Ry rotations + native CZ entanglers matching Rigetti Aspen topologies (Aspen-7/Aspen-8 sublattices; tested 4,6,8,10,12,28 qubits); number of parameters = n_qubits * layers; QCBM trained with Sinkhorn divergence (analytic gradients via parameter-shift), optimizer Adam (and vanilla GD in comparisons). RBM: visible nodes correspond to bits, hidden nodes chosen so RBM trainable parameter count matches QCBM; pairwise weights fixed random in many experiments and only local biases trained (they also experimented with training weights); RBM sampling via QxSQA (PIMC) or contrastive divergence variants; log-likelihood maximization used as RBM training objective. Evaluation: random-forest discriminator error, Sinkhorn divergence, QQ-plots, Meyer–Wallach entangling capability. Experiments run on simulators and on Rigetti QPUs (Aspen sublattices) via Rigetti QCS; multiple independent runs used to report mean/std.
dataset_used: FX spot prices (daily log-returns) for 4 currency pairs (time period 1999–2019), 5070 samples total. Data was discretized per currency pair to j-bit binary representations (j varied per experiment), producing binary vectors (e.g. 4 pairs x 16 bits = 64-bit vectors). Subsets of currency pairs (2,3,4) and different precisions (2..16 bits) were used to create problem instances.

Evaluate progress using random-forest discriminator error, Sinkhorn divergence, QQ plots of marginals, and Meyer–Wallach entangling capability of QCBM circuits.
Repeat experiments in classical simulation and run selected instances on Rigetti Aspen QPU(s) (including a 28-qubit run) using Rigetti QCS.

reproducibility_notes: The paper describes dataset sources (FX spot prices 1999-2019, 5070 samples) and preprocessing (daily log-returns, discretization to j-bit binary per currency pair). It specifies the QCBM ansatz family, cost functions (Sinkhorn divergence, MMD), gradient methods (parameter-shift), optimizer (Adam), and the use of Rigetti Aspen QPUs and QxSQA for sampling. However, the manuscript does not provide explicit public code or links to scripts, exact hyperparameter values (e.g., Adam learning rates, shot counts per circuit execution), nor seed values. Reproducing the results would therefore require reimplementation of the described training loops, ansatz details tied to Rigetti topologies, and access to Rigetti simulators/QPUs; absence of a code repository or explicit run scripts limits turnkey reproducibility.
key_findings: [supported] The authors implemented and compared a quantum circuit Born machine (QCBM) and a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) on a real-world FX financial dataset (5070 daily log-return samples, 1999–2019) converted to binary precision representations.

[supported] In simulation, the QCBM matched or outperformed the RBM on the generative modelling task when both models were constrained to have the same number of trainable parameters (biases for RBM; single-qubit rotations for QCBM).

[supported] The QCBM advantage increased as the discretisation precision of the currency pairs increased (examples reported: advantage emerging around 4 bits and more pronounced at 6 bits for 2 currency pairs; similar trends for 3 pairs), while for 4 pairs the advantage was less evident up to the studied precisions.

[supported] The Sinkhorn divergence was found (in the authors' experiments) to be an effective training cost for the QCBM, outperforming alternatives tried (MMD and adversarial discriminator) in speed/accuracy for these tasks.

[supported] The authors ran QCBM experiments on Rigetti hardware (Aspen-7 sublattices) and report having trained the largest-to-date QCBM on hardware (28 qubits on Aspen-7-28Q-4), observing learning despite hardware noise.

[supported] On the 28-qubit Rigetti run the QCBM showed measurable learning but worse performance than the RBM counterpart; the authors report discriminator error values up to ~20% for the hardware run (i.e., the model exhibited non-negligible discrepancies vs. data, attributed to hardware errors).

[supported] The authors observed a correlation between increased entangling-capability (Meyer–Wallach measure) of trained QCBM circuits and problem instances where the QCBM outperformed the RBM, suggesting entanglement plays a role in those instances.

[supported] Classical sampling for RBM training (they used a simulated QA sampler QxSQA) becomes a bottleneck as QCBM scale increases; classical simulation/time limits the number of training runs available.

[supported] Training the RBM weights (not just biases) can improve convergence and final accuracy in larger RBM instances (e.g., 28 visible nodes), but for many studied small instances adding hidden nodes/weights did not substantially change final outcomes.

[speculative] The paper reiterates the theoretical claim that Born machines have greater expressive power than some classical models and can represent certain distributions efficiently which classical models cannot (linking to ideas in quantum supremacy literature).

[speculative] The authors posit that quantum generative models are promising applications for NISQ-era devices and that entanglement/quantum properties likely underpin observed advantages in some datasets.

[speculative] The authors suggest performance degradation on hardware is 'likely' due to quantum errors (noise), and propose mitigation routes (error mitigation, parametric compilation, GPU-accelerated cost evaluation) as future work.
results_summary: The paper reports an empirical comparison between quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) for synthetic data generation on a converted FX dataset. Under a fairness constraint (matching the number of trainable parameters by restricting RBM training to biases and QCBM to single-qubit rotations), simulated QCBMs matched or outperformed RBMs, with the advantage becoming clearer as the discretisation precision increased (notably around 4–6 bits for small currency-pair subsets). The Sinkhorn divergence was used successfully as a training cost. The authors also ran QCBMs on Rigetti Aspen hardware up to 28 qubits, observing learning despite noise, though hardware performance lagged simulation (reported discriminator error up to ~20%). They observed that higher entangling capability of trained circuits correlates with instances where QCBMs outperform RBMs.
performance_claims: Dataset: 5070 samples of daily FX log-returns (1999–2019); pairs converted to 16-bit binary per pair (4 pairs -> 64-bit sample vectors).

Simulated QCBM outperforms or matches RBM when constrained to equal trainable parameters; advantage notable around 4 bits precision (2 currency pairs) and more pronounced at 6 bits in reported experiments.

For 3 currency pairs the QCBM showed similar advantageous trends at higher precisions (examples shown for 2 and 4 bits in the paper); for 4 currency pairs the advantage was not clearly observed up to 3 bits.

On Rigetti Aspen-7 hardware (28-qubit sublattice) the trained QCBM exhibited learning but performed worse than the (classical) RBM counterpart; the authors report discriminator error values up to approximately 20% for that hardware run.
A random-forest adversarial discriminator with 1000 estimators was used as the evaluation metric; higher discriminator error indicates better generator performance in this work.
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors present empirical simulations and limited hardware experiments where a QCBM matched or outperformed an RBM under constrained, fair parameter-count settings for specific financial-data instances and precisions. However, the results are task- and scale-specific (mostly simulation), hardware runs show degraded performance due to noise, and no general or provable quantum advantage is demonstrated; thus the claim remains preliminary/speculative.
limitations: Experiments limited to NISQ-era devices: hardware noise and errors on the Rigetti QPUs reduce QCBM performance (author-stated).
Classical simulation of QCBMs becomes a bottleneck as the model scales; largest (28-qubit) QCBM could not be fully simulated classically (author-stated).
RBM training in most experiments constrained to bias-only updates (weights fixed random) to match parameter counts, which limits the representational power of the classical baseline (author-stated).
Sample generation from RBMs is non-trivial and relies on approximate sampling methods (e.g., QA-simulated PIMC), potentially affecting RBM training quality (author-stated).

Training speed and wall-clock time are problematic: cost-function evaluation (Sinkhorn divergence etc.) and QPU execution time are slow; adversarial (GAN) training and genetic algorithms were significantly slower (author-stated).
Ansatz choices for the QCBM were constrained to hardware-efficient circuits with unparameterized two-qubit gates; this may limit expressivity or bias results (author-stated).

Limited exploration of classical baselines: study primarily compares QCBM to RBM (and variants); broader classical model comparisons (GANs, other implicit/explicit models) are not exhaustively tested (author-stated / suggested).
Discretization of continuous financial data to binary representations (fixed bit-precision) may lose information and restrict applicability to continuous-valued financial modelling (author-stated).
Performance on hardware at larger scales (28 qubits) was substantially degraded relative to ideal/simulated results, limiting claims about practical advantage (author-stated).
Use of specific cost functions (Sinkhorn divergence, MMD) and optimizers (Adam) — results may be sensitive to these choices and were not exhaustively compared (author-stated).
[inferred] Limited generalizability: experiments are performed on one financial dataset (FX spot returns) so transferability of conclusions to other financial instruments or domains is unclear.
[inferred] Correlation between increased entanglement and better performance observed, but causality and the conditions under which entanglement is necessary/sufficient are not established.

[inferred] The fairness constraint (matching number of trainable parameters) by restricting model structure may introduce bias: matching parameter counts does not guarantee matched capacity or inductive biases.
[inferred] Error mitigation and advanced compilation were not applied in depth; lack of such techniques may mask the QCBM's true potential on hardware.
[inferred] The study uses relatively small problem sizes for most experiments; it is unclear how both models behave on significantly larger, industry-scale problems.
[inferred] Resource/time cost and scalability of evaluating complex divergences (Sinkhorn) for many training iterations on larger models was not resolved and may limit practical use.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Simulated QCBMs matched or outperformed RBMs on the FX generative task (Sinkhorn divergence, discriminator error) as model scale and precision increased; higher circuit entanglement correlated with better performance.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Practical training used a hybrid workflow: parameter-shift analytic gradients on the QCBM, classical Adam optimizer, and classical discriminators for evaluation/adversarial training.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Authors performed experiments on Rigetti QPUs including partial training of a 28-qubit QCBM, demonstrating NISQ-era implementability (with caveats).

#limitation:qubit-count — Although a 28-qubit instance was executed, training was partial and experiments primarily focused on smaller instances (4–12 qubits), indicating limits to problem size handled in practice.
#limitation:noise — Hardware runs exhibited decreased performance relative to simulation, implicating noise and device errors as practical constraints on QCBM training and fidelity.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach requires discretizing continuous FX returns to j-bit binary vectors (nv = i * j), which increases visible-variable dimensionality and qubit requirements as precision or number of pairs grows, posing an encoding/scale cost.
contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The experimental comparison constrains the RBM by fixing pairwise weights randomly and training only biases (to match parameter counts), which may handicap the classical baseline; thus claims that QCBMs outperform RBMs could be driven by the fairness-constraint design rather than inherent model superiority.
